content: The World Health Organization (WHO) strongly recommends initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) for individuals with drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB), regardless of their CD4 cell count, as early as possible—ideally within the first eight weeks of starting anti-TB treatment. This recommendation is based on very low-certainty evidence. WHO has updated its guidelines on drug-resistant TB, including recommendations for treatment regimens for rifampicin-susceptible but isoniazid-resistant TB, shorter all-oral regimens containing bedaquiline for multidrug-resistant (MDR) or rifampicin-resistant TB, and longer regimens for MDR or rifampicin-resistant TB. There is potential for overlapping toxicities or drug-drug interactions between certain antiretroviral (ARV) drugs and injectable agents like moxifloxacin and clofazimine. However, these interactions generally do not necessitate modifications to MDR-TB or ART regimens. WHO advises against combining bedaquiline with efavirenz. ART regimens should be optimized and initiated early, following WHO recommendations, with close monitoring for treatment response and toxicity in individuals receiving both TB and HIV treatments. Comorbidities such as diabetes and mental health disorders should also be managed appropriately. Evidence from 10 studies assessing outcomes of combined ART and second-line anti-TB drugs was reviewed, though none were randomized controlled trials. Data from 217 individuals with drug-resistant TB, including 127 who received ART, showed low to very low certainty in observational studies. Latent TB infection (LTBI) is defined as a persistent immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens without clinical evidence of active TB disease. Approximately one-quarter of the global population is infected with TB. Among people living with HIV, combining TB preventive treatment with ART has shown benefits in reducing TB incidence and mortality, even in those with higher CD4 cell counts. WHO recommends TB preventive treatment for adults and adolescents living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB, as part of comprehensive HIV care. This includes individuals on ART, pregnant women, and those previously treated for TB, regardless of the degree of immunosuppression or availability of LTBI testing. Infants under 12 months living with HIV who have been in contact with a person with TB and are unlikely to have active TB should also receive preventive treatment. Children aged 12 months or older living with HIV in high TB transmission settings should be offered preventive treatment, even without known TB contact. WHO provides algorithms for ruling out active TB disease before initiating preventive treatment. Adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for TB using a clinical algorithm. Those without symptoms such as cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats are unlikely to have active TB and should be offered preventive treatment. Chest radiography may be used to rule out active TB in some cases. For latent TB infection, WHO recommends six or nine months of daily isoniazid, three months of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or three months of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. Alternatives include one month of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid or four months of daily rifampicin. In high TB transmission settings, adults and adolescents living with HIV should receive at least 36 months of daily isoniazid preventive therapy, regardless of ART status, immunosuppression, or pregnancy. Pregnancy should not exclude women living with HIV from receiving TB preventive treatment with medications like isoniazid and rifampicin, which are generally safe during pregnancy. For infants under 12 months, preventive treatment is recommended only for those with household TB contact and no active disease, due to limited data on benefits. Drug-drug interactions between rifamycins (e.g., rifampicin) and ARVs should be carefully managed. Rifampicin can reduce the concentrations of certain protease inhibitors (PIs) and other ARVs, but no dose adjustment is needed when co-administered with efavirenz. Dolutegravir (DTG) dosing should be increased to 50 mg twice daily when used with rifampicin, continuing for two weeks after stopping rifampicin. Hepatitis B (HBV) and hepatitis C (HCV) infections are significant comorbidities among people living with HIV. HBV is often acquired perinatally or in early childhood, while HCV transmission is commonly associated with unsafe injection practices and high-risk behaviors. Coinfection with HIV accelerates liver disease progression, increasing the risk of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and mortality. Early diagnosis and treatment of viral hepatitis are critical for people living with HIV. Testing for HBV and HCV is essential for accessing prevention and treatment services. WHO recommends focused testing for populations at higher risk, including people living with HIV, people who inject drugs, and individuals in high-prevalence settings. For HCV, testing should include an antibody test followed by RNA or core antigen testing to confirm active infection. For HBV, serological testing for HBsAg is recommended, particularly for pregnant women in antenatal care. Direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy for HCV is safe and effective for people with HIV-HCV coinfection, with outcomes comparable to those without HIV. However, drug-drug interactions between DAAs and ARVs must be carefully managed. WHO emphasizes the importance of ART stabilization before initiating HCV treatment, particularly for individuals with advanced immunosuppression. WHO guidelines provide detailed recommendations for managing these coinfections, including the use of simplified public health approaches to testing and treatment.
